# Evaluation

**2026-09-02** · generated by `scripts/11_run_evaluation.py` · no API calls

What the pipeline's own numbers can and cannot support. The order below is
the order of evidential weight, and the first section is the one that
determines how every other number in this project should be read.

---

## 1. Ground truth

**No accuracy figure exists for this pipeline.**

The gold set has been sampled and the annotation sheet generated, but
no human has labelled it. Until that happens, every label-quality
number this project reports — including the 98.4% grounding rate — is a
statement about *internal consistency*, not about correctness.

Concretely, the following remain unmeasured:

- whether a review labelled `late_delivery` is about a late delivery
- whether the areas the model omits are areas a person would have found
- whether sentiment tracks what the customer actually expressed

To fix it: `python scripts/10_build_goldset.py`, fill in the template,
save it as `data/eval/gold_labels.csv`, and re-run this script. The
sections below will change from italics to numbers.

The sheet is ready: `data/eval/gold_template.csv`, 134 reviews, none labelled yet.

---

## 2. What the validators actually catch

The run report says 98.4% of evidence spans verified. That is a statement
about what the detectors *found*, and on its own it is equally consistent
with a careful model or a blind detector. This section injects known faults
into enrichments the pipeline already accepted and measures what its own
validators make of them.

**2138 of 2138 injected faults were caught — 100.0% (99.8–100.0).**

| Fault | Defence | Injected | Capture rate | Attributed correctly |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quote invented outright | grounding | 200 | 100.0% (98.1–100.0) | 100.0% |
| Quote missing an interior word | grounding | 176 | 100.0% (97.9–100.0) | 100.0% |
| Two fragments joined by an ellipsis | schema | 184 | 100.0% (98.0–100.0) | 100.0% |
| Category not in the taxonomy | taxonomy | 200 | 100.0% (98.1–100.0) | 100.0% |
| Real issue type under the wrong area | taxonomy | 179 | 100.0% (97.9–100.0) | 100.0% |
| Issue and strength on one label | taxonomy | 199 | 100.0% (98.1–100.0) | 100.0% |
| Area named with neither issue nor strength | taxonomy | 200 | 100.0% (98.1–100.0) | 100.0% |
| Attribute outside the enum | taxonomy | 200 | 100.0% (98.1–100.0) | 100.0% |
| Identical label repeated | taxonomy | 200 | 100.0% (98.1–100.0) | 100.0% |
| Confidence above 1.0 | schema | 200 | 100.0% (98.1–100.0) | 100.0% |
| Answer echoes an id nobody requested | reconciliation | 200 | 100.0% (98.1–100.0) | 100.0% |

*Capture rate* is whether any validator objected at all. *Attributed
correctly* is whether the validator that owns that fault class was the one
that fired — a fault caught by the wrong defence is still caught, but the
defence responsible for it has a hole. Every subject is drawn from the
enrichments that already validate cleanly, so anything raised after
mutation is unambiguously the study's doing.

### The control

Run over **untouched** enrichments, the same validators flagged 9.2% (8.3–10.0).

This is the half of the result that a capture rate alone hides: a
validator that raised on everything would score 100% above and be
worthless. What fires on input nobody touched:

- `ungrounded_evidence` — 156
- `missing_polarity` — 117
- `unknown_issue_type` — 115
- `duplicate_label` — 41
- `unknown_strength_type` — 3
- `conflicting_polarity` — 1

These are real residual issues in stored enrichments, not false alarms
created by the study. They are also the reason the study injects only
into the **4150 of 4568** enrichments
that validate cleanly: damaging a label the validators were already
flagging tells you nothing, and would be scored as a miss because the
verdict could not change.

### How much of this is worth anything

A table of 100% capture rates should raise suspicion rather than
confidence, so it is worth separating the rows that are near-tautological
from the rows that are not.

**Close to tautological.** Out-of-enum sentiment and out-of-range confidence
are caught by Pydantic because Pydantic is a schema validator and they are
schema violations. The ellipsis check likewise fires on the character it
exists to look for. These rows confirm the wiring, and nothing else.

**Genuinely informative.** Three cases require a check that a schema cannot
perform:

- *A real issue type filed under the wrong area.* Both values are in the
  enum; only the parent–child relationship is wrong. Nothing but the
  taxonomy graph can see it.
- *An answer echoing an id nobody requested.* Caught by reconciliation, not
  validation. Undetected, this is the worst fault in the set — every label
  lands on the wrong review and the dataset is misaligned rather than merely
  wrong.
- *A quote missing one interior word.* No ellipsis to spot and no schema
  violation; only substring matching stands between it and the dataset.
  This is the closest analogue to what a model actually does when it tidies
  a quote instead of copying it, and the one row where a miss would have
  been most expected.

### The limit of this study

Injected faults are synthetic, so these are **upper bounds** on real-world
detection: a mutation designed to represent an error class is generally
cruder than the errors a model actually makes. What the study establishes
is that each defence fires on the class of error it was built for and stays
quiet otherwise — not that no undetectable failure mode exists.

---

## 2b. What the validators do *not* do

The section above measures whether an error is **detected**. This one asks
what happened next, and the answer is not what the run report implies:

> **The validators report. They do not gate.**

`parse_and_validate` records an issue and then appends the enrichment
anyway. That is defensible — dropping a review because one of its three
labels is misfiled discards two good labels and a whole row of coverage —
but it means "N invalid issue types were found" and "N invalid issue types
are in the dataset" are the same sentence, and nothing said so.

Of **10,790** shipped labels, **10,476** are fully valid.

| Invalid label | Count | Share | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Issue type absent from the taxonomy, or filed under the wrong area | 116 | 1.1% (0.9–1.3) | counts toward a pain point that the taxonomy does not define |
| Strength type absent from the taxonomy, or filed under the wrong area | 3 | 0.0% (0.0–0.1) | inflates the praise side of an area it does not belong to |
| Area named with neither an issue nor a strength | 195 | 1.8% (1.6–2.1) | carries no product meaning; excluded from every issue-side analysis |

None of these move a published figure today: every downstream analysis
filters to issue-polarity labels, and an invalid issue type forms its own
small group rather than contaminating a valid one. They are reported
because a reader has no way to discover them otherwise, and because the
next analysis to read the strength side would inherit all of them.

### The taxonomy's own monitoring rule

`config/taxonomy.yaml` states a rule for `general_no_specific_area` that had never
been evaluated against a full run:

> If LLM classification assigns this to more than 10% of reviews, the taxonomy has a real gap and must be revisited before the results are trusted.

**Measured: 1.6%** (75 reviews) against a threshold of 10% — well clear. The taxonomy covers this corpus.

### Grounding, recounted from the dataset

156 of 4,568 reviews carry at least one span that does not appear verbatim in their text (3.4% (2.9–4.0)); mean rate 98.37%.

Counted from `reviews_enriched.parquet` rather than from the run report,
which is a distinction that mattered: cache hits used to bypass grounding
verification entirely and were written out as a perfect 1.0. The two
numbers now agree because the enrichment path re-verifies a cached
answer, which costs nothing — grounding is a property of the text, not
of the request that fetched it.

## 3. Retrieval

Every root-cause hypothesis is built from retrieved evidence, so a retriever
returning plausible but off-topic reviews would produce hypotheses that cite
real ids, pass the citation check, and mean nothing.

**Pooled precision@8: 77.5% (69.2–84.1)** against a mean base rate of 15.0% — a mean lift of 6.6×. 14 of 15 areas beat their base rate with the interval clear of it.

| Area | Support | Precision@k | Base rate | Lift | Clears base rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `availability_and_range` | 519 | 100.0% (67.6–100.0) | 11.4% | 8.8× | yes |
| `customer_support` | 1845 | 100.0% (67.6–100.0) | 40.4% | 2.5× | yes |
| `delivery_reliability` | 1412 | 100.0% (67.6–100.0) | 30.9% | 3.2× | yes |
| `order_lifecycle` | 679 | 100.0% (67.6–100.0) | 14.9% | 6.7× | yes |
| `pricing_and_charges` | 515 | 100.0% (67.6–100.0) | 11.3% | 8.9× | yes |
| `app_experience` | 1298 | 87.5% (52.9–97.8) | 28.4% | 3.1× | yes |
| `refunds` | 615 | 87.5% (52.9–97.8) | 13.5% | 6.5× | yes |
| `wallet_and_credits` | 515 | 87.5% (52.9–97.8) | 11.3% | 7.8× | yes |
| `offers_and_promotions` | 301 | 75.0% (40.9–92.9) | 6.6% | 11.4× | yes |
| `payments` | 209 | 75.0% (40.9–92.9) | 4.6% | 16.4× | yes |
| `product_quality` | 669 | 75.0% (40.9–92.9) | 14.6% | 5.1× | yes |
| `order_fulfilment` | 734 | 62.5% (30.6–86.3) | 16.1% | 3.9× | yes |
| `returns_and_replacement` | 369 | 62.5% (30.6–86.3) | 8.1% | 7.7× | yes |
| `delivery_partner_conduct` | 365 | 37.5% (13.7–69.4) | 8.0% | 4.7× | yes |
| `serviceability` | 234 | 12.5% (2.2–47.1) | 5.1% | 2.4× | no |

Queries are generated from each area's own name and definition in
`config/taxonomy.yaml`, not hand-written — a tuned query set measures the
person who tuned it. Search is run **unfiltered**; passing the area as a
filter would return precision 1.0 by construction.

**The weak row is `serviceability`, and inspecting its hits
gives the mechanism.** The misses are not random: they are reviews about
*customer service* and *delivery service*. The area is named for an
operations concept whose word stem means something entirely different in
customer language, and a query generated from that name inherits the
collision — the embedding matches the word, not the concept.

That is a **taxonomy naming** finding rather than a retrieval one, and it
predicts the rest of the table: the areas that score highest are the ones
whose names are the words customers actually use for them. Where an area's
vocabulary collides with a commoner sense, evidence for it should be
gathered with the label filter rather than by semantic search alone.

**What this is not.** The reference is the pipeline's own labels, so this
measures agreement between two independent systems — MiniLM embeddings and
a 70B labeller that never see each other's output — rather than relevance
as a person would judge it. It is real evidence about consistency and no
evidence at all about truth.

## 4. Inter-model agreement

Reproduced from the per-model caches rather than computed by hand, so
`docs/MODEL_BENCHMARK.md` quotes a computation instead of a memory.

### `llama70b` vs `qwen72b` — 95 reviews in common

Coverage differs: 4473 reviews only `llama70b` labelled, 0 only `qwen72b`. Those are reported here and excluded from the scores, because a review one model never reached is a coverage fact, not a disagreement.

| Comparison | Value |
|---|---|
| Product area — F1 | 0.882 |
| Product area — exact set match | 61.1% (51.0–70.2) |
| Product area — mean Jaccard | 0.825 |
| Area + type — F1 | 0.678 |
| Areas per review | 2.29 vs 2.34 |

| Field | Agreement | Majority baseline | Cohen's κ |
|---|---|---|---|
| `customer_intent` | 90.5% (83.0–94.9) | 78.9% | 0.714 |
| `sentiment` | 96.8% (91.1–98.9) | 71.6% | 0.928 |
| `severity` | 62.5% (51.5–72.3) | 41.2% | 0.425 |
| `support_escalation` | 89.5% (81.7–94.2) | 67.4% | 0.779 |

**Agreement is not accuracy.** Two models can be wrong in the same way,
and where they differ at least one is wrong without this saying which.
The serialised artefact carries `is_accuracy: false` for exactly this
reason — so a downstream reader cannot pick the number up and relabel it.

The κ column is what makes the sentiment figure readable. Raw agreement is
high partly because the corpus is overwhelmingly negative and both models
say so; κ removes that.

Where agreement is *lowest* is where the gold set should be spent, which is
what the disagreement stratum in `scripts/10_build_goldset.py` consumes.

---

## What this evaluation licenses

| Claim | Supported? |
|---|---|
| An invalid label is *detected* | **yes** — capture rate measured in §2 |
| An invalid label is *excluded* from the dataset | **no** — see §2b; validation reports, it does not gate |
| A response about the wrong review cannot enter the dataset | **yes** — reconciliation is measured above |
| Retrieval returns reviews about the query rather than noise | **partly** — consistent with the labels, not with a human judgement |
| Two models agree about what a review is about | **measured, and often they do not** |
| The labels are *correct* | **unmeasured — no gold set** |

The last row is the one that matters, and the framework around it is built
so that filling it in requires a person rather than another model. Generating
the reference with an LLM would produce an accuracy number for free and it
would be measuring one model's agreement with another, which is section 4,
which is already here.
